<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Jahana Hayes, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
The Charter School Program (CSP) is authorized by the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965 (ESEA)\1\ for the purpose of ``supporting innovation; providing financial assistance for the planning, design, and initial implementation of charter schools; increasing the number of high-quality charter schools; encouraging states to provide charter schools facilities financing; and strengthening the charter school authorizing process.''\2\ H.R. 7082, the Fostering Learning and Excellence in Charter Schools (FLEX) Act, introduced by Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-PA),\3\ would alter CSP by shifting reserved funds for different sections of the program, expanding the allowable uses of funds under the supporting high-quality charter schools section of the program, and eliminating oversight provisions, among other things.\4\ By doing so, the bill would significantly reduce funding for high-quality charter schools, reduce guardrails and transparency, and open the door for potentially greater waste, fraud, and abuse in the program.\5\
\1\20 U.S.C. Sec. Sec. 7221-7221j.
\2\Rebecca R. Skinner & Isobel Sorenson, Cong. Rsch. Serv., IF12601, ESEA: Charter Schools Program, (2024), https://www.crs.gov/ Reports/IF12601; see 20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221(1)-(8).
\3\Fostering Learning and Excellence in Charter Schools (FLEX) Act, H.R. 7082, 119th Cong. (2026).
\4\Id.
\5\Id.
SUMMARY OF CONCERNS
H.R. 7082 Would Slash Funding and Erode Safeguards for the High-Quality
Charter Schools Section of CSP
H.R. 7082 Would Slash Funding for High-Quality Charter
Schools
Pursuant to current law, CSP authorizes funds to support charter schools in three ways, and each of these ways has its own specific funding set-aside/reservation:\6\ supporting high-quality charter schools (65% of CSP funds);\7\ facilities financing assistance (12.5% of CSP funds);\8\ and national activities (22.5% of CSP funds).\9\ H.R. 7082 would change the amounts reserved for each of the three sections.\10\ Specifically, the bill would: (1) increase the reservation of funds for facilities financing assistance from 12.5 to 15 percent;\11\ (2) increase the amount reserved for national activities from 22.5 to 25 percent;\12\ and (3) reduce the amount of funds reserved for supporting high-quality charter schools from 65 to ``at least 30 percent'' and allow the remaining 35 percent to be distributed among all three sections as determined by the Secretary.\13\ The latter change is the most significant. Republicans assert that H.R. 7082 would ``reduce red tape and provide greater flexibility [in CSP] . . . ensuring resources reach classrooms more efficiently and respond to the needs of students and families.''\14\ In fact, H.R. 7082 would do the opposite. Rather than continue to emphasize supporting high-quality charter schools as CSP currently does, the bill would allow funding for high-quality charter schools to be reduced by more than half. It would permit the Secretary to more than triple the amount of funds used for facilities financing assistance and more than double the amount used for national activities. As a result, significantly less funding would go directly to students, families, and classrooms.
\6\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221a(a)-(b); Skinner, supra note 2.
\7\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221a(b)(3). This funding provides grants to State Entities (defined as state educational agencies (SEAs), state governors, state charter school authorizing boards, or charter school support organizations), which in turn provide subgrants to eligible applicants (defined as charter school developers that have applied to a charter authorizer to open a charter school) to open a new charter school or replicate or expand a high-quality charter school. 20 U.S.C.
Sec. 7221b.
\8\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7721a(b)(1). This reservation funds two types of programs: (1) Credit Enhancement Grants, which ``are made to public or private entities (or a combination of the two) for the development of credit enhancement initiatives to assist charter schools in acquiring, constructing, or renovating facilities''; and (2) Facilities Incentive Grants (also called Per-Pupil Facilities Grants or the Per-Pupil Facilities Aid Program), which ``provide[] funds to states to establish or enhance and administer per-pupil facilities allowances to help charter schools obtain facilities'' in states that permit such per-pupil facilities aid. Skinner, supra note 2; 20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221c.
\9\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7721a(b)(2). This reservation funds: (1) Replication and Expansion of High-Quality Charter Schools Grants, which provide funding to non-profit Charter Management Organizations ``to replicate or expand one or more high-quality charter schools''; (2) Developer Grants, which are provided to ``charter school developers in states that do not have a current CSP grant to a state entity [and] may apply directly to the Secretary of Education (the Secretary) for a competitive grant to open a new charter school or replicate or expand a high-quality charter school; and (3) Dissemination and Evaluation Grants to provide technical assistance, disseminate best practices, and evaluate the impact of CSP, including its impact on student achievement. Skinner, supra note 2; 20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221d.
\10\H.R. 7082 Sec. 2, 119th Cong. (2026).
\11\Id.
\12\Id.
\13\Id.
\14\Press Release, Congressman Mackenzie's FLEX Act Advances Through Committee (Jan. 21, 2026), https://mackenzie.house.gov/media/ press-releases/congressman-mackenzies-flex-act-advances-through-committee.
H.R. 7082 would also expand the allowable uses of funds authorized to support high-quality charter schools in the CSP. The bill would permit funding under that section to be used for ``curricular or other offerings,'' ``new academic programs or delivery models,'' ``personalized learning,'' or ``a new curricular approach.''\15\ However, the bill does not define these terms, and it is unclear what they mean or how they could be interpreted by the Department of Education (Department). Thus, the bill would significantly reduce the funds that may be available for high-quality charter schools while at the same time dilute what the remaining funds may be used for by inserting these new and amorphous terms. The bill states that this change must done in a way that would ``enable additional students to enroll in and benefit from the school,'' but as written, the language would be satisfied with the enrollment of only two additional students, and how the term ``benefit'' would be assessed is unclear.
\15\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
H.R. 7082 Would Eliminate Oversight by the Secretary
Current law requires that the Secretary conduct interim reviews of grants to state entities to ensure a grant is being used appropriately and determine whether the full grant amount will be needed; based on that review, the Secretary may reduce or terminate the grant.\16\ H.R. 7082 would eliminate this oversight review.\17\
\16\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(d)(3).
\17\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
Research has shown that some CSP funds awarded to plan and open charter schools are used by entities that either never ultimately open a charter school or open a school and close it shortly thereafter.\18\ In fact, data has shown that charter schools close at a much higher rate than traditional public schools. More than 25 percent of charter schools close within five years of opening, and this increases to 49 percent within fifteen years of opening.\19\ According to then-Secretary of Education Betsy DeVos, from school year 2006-2007 to school year 2013-2014, $70,000,000 in CSP funding was provided to 634 charter schools that did not open or were not likely to open.\20\ More recently, from school year 2022-23 to school year 2023-24, there were 218 ``charter schools that closed or never opened.''\21\
\18\Peter Greene, Report: The Department Of Education Has Spent $1 Billion On Charter School Waste And Fraud, Forbes (Mar. 29, 2019), https://www.forbes.com/sites/petergreene/2019/03/29/report-the-department-of-education-has-spent-1-billion-on-charter-school-waste-and-fraud/; Network for Pub. Educ., Still Asleep at the Wheel: How the Federal Charter Schools Program Results in a Pileup of Fraud and Waste (rev. Jan. 2020), https://networkforpubliceducation.org/wp-content/ uploads/2025/06/Still-Asleep-at-the-Wheel.pdf; Nat'l Ctr. for Charter Sch. Accountability & Network for Pub. Educ., Doomed to Fail: An Analysis of Charter School Closures from 1998 to 2022 (Nov. 2024), https://networkforpubliceducation.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/DTM- Final.pdf; Nat'l Ctr. for Charter Sch. Accountability & Network for Pub. Educ., Charter School Reckoning: Decline, Disillusionment and Cost, Part I: Decline (July 2025), https:// networkforpubliceducation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Charter- School-Reckoning-FINAL-1.pdf.
\19\Doomed to Fail, supra note 18, at 2.
\20\Letter from the Honorable Betsy DeVos, Sec'y, U.S. Dep't of Educ., responding to oversight request regarding the Charter Schools Program, to the Honorable Ral M. Grijalva, Member of Congress (June 28, 2019) (on file with the Comm. on Educ. and Workforce Min. Staff); see also Still Asleep at the Wheel, supra note 18, at 2 (stating that the numbers for that same time period are much higher--$502,468,123 was awarded to schools that never opened or opened and closed).
\21\Charter School Reckoning, supra note 18, at 6.
Charter schools generally close due to low enrollment (which impacts their funding directly) or fraud and mismanagement.\22\ Some charter supporters believe that ``school closures are considered a natural consequence of the marketplace model.''\23\ But failure at this alarmingly high rate has a substantial impact on students and their families. Unfortunately, this occurs even with the oversight included in current law. By removing this oversight provision, H.R. 7082 would open the door to further misuse of funds and harm to students and families.
\22\Still Asleep at the Wheel, supra note 18, at 26-27.
\23\Doomed to Fail, supra note 18, at 5.
H.R. 7082 Would Eliminate State Entity Reporting and
Oversight
Current law requires that each state entity that receives a grant submit an interim and a final report to the Secretary.\24\ The law further delineates what must be included in the report, including: the number and amount of subgrants awarded; the number of students served by each subgrant as well as the number of new students served each year of the subgrant; and how the state entity met the objectives in its grant application.\25\ H.R. 7082 would eliminate the interim report.\26\ In so doing, it would eliminate the need for the state entity to conduct oversight of its subgrantees and report back to the Secretary as well as eliminate a tool the Secretary may use in its own evaluation of the state entity and determination of whether to reduce or terminate the state entity's grant. This provision of the bill would eradicate an entire chain of oversight and transparency.
\24\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(i).
\25\Id.
\26\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
H.R. 7082 Would Emphasize Obligating Funds Quickly Over
Quality and Oversight of the Program
Current law permits the Secretary to award one grant at a time to any state entity.\27\ In contrast, H.R. 7082 would permit the Secretary to award additional grants as long as the funding for an existing grant has been obligated.\28\ This change would encourage state entities to obligate funding as quickly as possible in order to remove any barrier to receiving a new grant award. Combined with the elimination of the Secretary's oversight review of such grants, there is no mechanism to ensure responsible allocation and spending of a grant award.
\27\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(e)(1).
\28\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
